documents.title: Sodium-glucose co-transporter protein 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors for people with chronic kidney disease and diabetes.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Diabetes is associated with high risks of premature chronic kidney disease (CKD), cardiovascular diseases, cardiovascular death and impaired quality of life. People with diabetes are more likely to develop kidney impairment, and approximately one in three adults with diabetes have CKD. People with CKD and diabetes experience a substantially higher risk of cardiovascular outcomes. Sodium-glucose co-transporter protein 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors have shown potential effects in preventing kidney and cardiovascular outcomes in people with CKD and diabetes. However, new trials are emerging rapidly, and evidence synthesis is essential to summarising cumulative evidence.
OBJECTIVES: This review aimed to assess the benefits and harms of SGLT2 inhibitors for people with CKD and diabetes.
SEARCH METHODS: We searched the Cochrane Kidney and Transplant Register of Studies up to 17 November 2023 using a search strategy designed by an Information Specialist. Studies in the Register are continually identified through regular searches of CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, conference proceedings, the International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP) Search Portal and ClinicalTrials.gov.
SELECTION CRITERIA: Randomised controlled studies were eligible if they evaluated SGLT2 inhibitors versus placebo, standard care or other glucose-lowering agents in people with CKD and diabetes. CKD includes all stages (from 1 to 5), including dialysis patients.
DATA COLLECTION AND ANALYSIS: Two authors independently extracted data and assessed the study risk of bias. Treatment estimates were summarised using random effects meta-analysis and expressed as a risk ratio (RR) or mean difference (MD), with a corresponding 95% confidence interval (CI). Confidence in the evidence was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach. The primary review outcomes were all-cause death, 3-point and 4-point major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), fatal or nonfatal myocardial infarction (MI), fatal or nonfatal stroke, and kidney failure.
MAIN RESULTS: Fifty-three studies randomising 65,241 people with CKD and diabetes were included. SGLT2 inhibitors with or without other background treatments were compared to placebo, standard care, sulfonylurea, dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitors, or insulin. In the majority of domains, the risks of bias in the included studies were low or unclear. No studies evaluated the treatment in children or in people treated with dialysis. No studies compared SGLT2 inhibitors with glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists or tirzepatide. Compared to placebo, SGLT2 inhibitors decreased the risk of all-cause death (20 studies, 44,397 participants: RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.78 to 0.94; I2 = 0%; high certainty) and cardiovascular death (16 studies, 43,792 participants: RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.74 to 0.93; I2 = 29%; high certainty). Compared to placebo, SGLT2 inhibitors probably make little or no difference to the risk of fatal or nonfatal MI (2 studies, 13,726 participants: RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.14; I2 = 24%; moderate certainty), and fatal or nonfatal stroke (2 studies, 13,726 participants: RR 1.07, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.30; I2 = 0%; moderate certainty). Compared to placebo, SGLT2 inhibitors probably decrease 3-point MACE (7 studies, 38,320 participants: RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.81 to 0.98; I2 = 46%; moderate certainty), and 4-point MACE (4 studies, 23,539 participants: RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.70 to 0.96; I2 = 77%; moderate certainty), and decrease hospital admission due to heart failure (6 studies, 28,339 participants: RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.79; I2 = 17%; high certainty). Compared to placebo, SGLT2 inhibitors may decrease creatinine clearance (1 study, 132 participants: MD -2.63 mL/min, 95% CI -5.19 to -0.07; low certainty) and probably decrease the doubling of serum creatinine (2 studies, 12,647 participants: RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.89; I2 = 53%; moderate certainty). SGLT2 inhibitors decrease the risk of kidney failure (6 studies, 11,232 participants: RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.79; I2 = 0%; high certainty), and kidney composite outcomes (generally reported as kidney failure, kidney death with or without ≥ 40% decrease in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)) (7 studies, 36,380 participants: RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.78; I2 = 25%; high certainty) compared to placebo. Compared to placebo, SGLT2 inhibitors incur less hypoglycaemia (16 studies, 28,322 participants: RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.89 to 0.98; I2 = 0%; high certainty), and hypoglycaemia requiring third-party assistance (14 studies, 26,478 participants: RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.88; I2 = 0%; high certainty), and probably decrease the withdrawal from treatment due to adverse events (15 studies, 16,622 participants: RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.08; I2 = 16%; moderate certainty). The effects of SGLT2 inhibitors on eGFR, amputation and fracture were uncertain. No studies evaluated the effects of treatment on fatigue, life participation, or lactic acidosis. The effects of SGLT2 inhibitors compared to standard care alone, sulfonylurea, DPP-4 inhibitors, or insulin were uncertain.
AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: SGLT2 inhibitors alone or added to standard care decrease all-cause death, cardiovascular death, and kidney failure and probably decrease major cardiovascular events while incurring less hypoglycaemia compared to placebo in people with CKD and diabetes.

documents.title: Interventions for treating COVID-19 in people with chronic kidney disease.
documents.abstract: OBJECTIVES: This is a protocol for a Cochrane Review (intervention). The objectives are as follows: To assess the benefits and harms of interventions for treating coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) in people with all chronic kidney disease (CKD) stages, including those undergoing dialysis and kidney transplant recipients.

Objectives This is a protocol for a Cochrane Review (intervention). The objectives are as follows: To assess the benefits and harms of interventions for treating coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID‐19) in people with all chronic kidney disease (CKD) stages, including those undergoing dialysis and kidney transplant recipients. status released display-pdf yes is-olf no is-manuscript no is-preprint no is-journal-matter no is-scanned no is-retracted no Collection date 2026. Background Description of the condition Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID‐19), caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS‐CoV‐2), has been recognised as a multisystem disease that leads to respiratory failure, multiorgan dysfunction, fatigue, dyspnoea, impaired functional status, and related conditions such as acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), blood clot complications (thromboembolic disease), myocarditis, and secondary bacterial or fungal infections [ 1 , 2 ]. By 2024, over 700 million confirmed cases and millions of deaths had been recorded worldwide [ 3 ]. Although global incidence has declined, COVID‐19 continues to place a substantial burden on the health system, especially in people with chronic conditions [ 4 ]. Chronic kidney disease (CKD) affects more than 850 million people globally, and its prevalence is increasing, especially in the elderly or in those experiencing hypertension, diabetes, and obesity [ 5 ]. People with CKD, including those receiving any form of dialysis or kidney transplant recipients, are at disproportionately higher risk of severe outcomes related to COVID‐19, including acute kidney injury (AKI), prolonged hospitalisation, intensive care admission, and death [ 6 , 7 ]. Furthermore, people with CKD are also more susceptible to prolonged release of virus particles from the body (viral shedding), higher viral loads, and secondary infections such as hospital‐acquired infections [ 8 ], and their immune dysregulation creates a unique way the body responds to infection (host‐pathogen interaction profile), leading not only to severe primary COVID‐19 but also to infectious complications that compound morbidity and death [ 9 ]. Despite this heightened vulnerability, current guidelines for treating COVID‐19 have been developed based on data from the general population that may show a different effectiveness compared to people with CKD due to their immune dysregulation, systemic inflammation, and immunosuppressive therapy [ 10 ]. Description of the intervention and how it might work In recent years, a variety of interventions have been used to treat COVID‐19 in people with CKD. These include antiviral agents (e.g. remdesivir and nirmatrelvir/ritonavir) that inhibit viral replication by targeting viral enzymes essential for replication [ 11 ], neutralising monoclonal antibodies (e.g. casirivimab/imdevimab, tixagevimab/cilgavimab) that bind to the SARS‐CoV‐2 spike protein to prevent viral entry into host cells [ 12 , 13 ], and anti‐inflammatory drugs (e.g. corticosteroids) that suppress pro‐inflammatory cytokines and reduce immune‐mediated tissue damage [ 14 ]. Additionally, medicines that block specific inflammatory proteins in the immune system (interleukin (IL) inhibitors (e.g. tocilizumab, anakinra)) specifically block cytokine signalling pathways involved in inflammation, such as IL‐6 or IL‐1 [ 15 ], while immunomodulators (e.g. baricitinib, a Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor) interfere with intracellular signalling to dampen the hyperinflammatory response [ 16 , 17 ]. Antimalarials (e.g. hydroxychloroquine) have also been explored for their potential to inhibit viral entry by increasing acidity within small cellular compartments (endosomal pH) and altering chemical sugar modifications on cell surface receptors (receptor glycosylation), although their clinical benefit remains unproven in this population [ 11 ]. Treatment choices depend on both the severity and timing of COVID‐19 infection and the underlying CKD stage, including any form of kidney replacement therapy (KRT) such as dialysis or kidney transplantation [ 18 ]. Key subgroups of interest in COVID‐19 treatment include different age groups—given that older adults with CKD are at higher risk of severe disease—and timing of treatment initiation, as early antiviral therapy may improve outcomes, whereas delayed therapy may reduce efficacy. There are several issues in treating COVID‐19 patients with CKD: firstly, these patients may receive delayed treatment with antivirals due to drug–drug interactions or renal dosing restrictions. Secondly, corticosteroids, JAK inhibitors, and IL inhibitors improve outcomes in severe disease but increase susceptibility to secondary and opportunistic infections, including tuberculosis, hepatitis B reactivation, and invasive fungal infections. This infectious risk is magnified in CKD patients with pre‐existing immune dysfunction. These therapeutic approaches aim to reduce viral replication, control excessive immune responses, and prevent or manage complications such as respiratory failure, thromboembolism, or AKI [ 19 ]. These interventions also balance risks of prolonged viral shedding, nosocomial infections, and opportunistic pathogens, which are significantly relevant to the CKD population. Why it is important to do this review Current COVID‐19 treatment guidelines are mainly based on studies conducted in the general population and may not adequately reflect the clinical profile of individuals with CKD [ 20 ]. Factors such as altered immune function, chronic inflammation, the use of immunosuppressive therapies, and impaired drug metabolism due to reduced kidney function may significantly affect both the safety and efficacy of COVID‐19 treatments in this population [ 21 , 22 , 23 ]. Consequently, significant evidence gaps remain regarding the proper management of COVID‐19 in people with CKD, posing challenges for clinical decision‐making. This review aims to systematically synthesise evidence on COVID‐19 interventions in people with CKD. These findings will support tailored clinical decisions, guide policymakers and healthcare providers in optimising treatment strategies, and improve patient outcomes while promoting efficient use of healthcare resources. The clinical course and severity of COVID‐19 have evolved over time due to changes in circulating viral variants, availability of vaccination, and improvements in supportive care. Treatment effects may therefore vary according to age group, timing of treatment initiation, pandemic wave (reflecting circulating variants), dominant viral variant, and vaccination availability. These factors may influence both disease severity and response to therapy and should be considered when interpreting trial results. Objectives To assess the benefits and harms of interventions for treating coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID‐19) in people with all chronic kidney disease (CKD) stages, including those undergoing dialysis and kidney transplant recipients. Methods Criteria for considering studies for this review Types of studies We will include all randomised clinical trials (RCTs) and quasi‐randomised clinical trials (i.e. studies in which allocation to treatment is determined by alternation, use of alternate medical records, date of birth, or other systematic approaches), cluster‐RCTs, and cross‐over RCTs. Eligible studies will evaluate the effects of pharmacological interventions for COVID‐19 (e.g. antiviral agents, neutralising monoclonal antibodies, IL inhibitors, immunomodulators, and antimalarial drugs) compared with placebo, standard care, or no treatment in people with CKD, regardless of the duration of follow‐up. Types of participants We will include adults and children with CKD at any stage (1 to 5), as defined by the Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) guidelines [ 24 ]. CKD will be classified according to C ause, G lomerular filtration rate (GFR) category, and A lbuminuria category (CGA classification). This includes individuals with a reduced estimated GFR (eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73 m² for ≥ 3 months), or those with normal or mildly decreased eGFR (≥ 60 mL/min/1.73 m²) and evidence of kidney damage, such as persistent albuminuria (e.g. urinary albumin excretion ≥ 30 mg/day or ≥ 30 mg/g creatinine), structural abnormalities of the kidney, or a documented primary kidney diagnosis (e.g. diabetic kidney disease, glomerulonephritis, hereditary kidney disorders). Participants must have confirmed or suspected SARS‐CoV‐2 infection, and, where reported, data on viral variant, vaccination status, and prior infection will be extracted, given their infectious‐disease relevance. We will include individuals receiving KRT, including haemodialysis (HD), peritoneal dialysis (PD), or kidney transplantation, irrespective of modality, frequency, or duration. Participants may have CKD of any underlying cause, with or without comorbidities or complications (e.g. hypertension, diabetes). Studies that include mixed populations (e.g. participants with and without CKD) will be eligible, but outcome data will be extracted only if they are specifically related to the CKD subgroup. We will exclude studies that focus exclusively on populations with AKI, normal kidney function, or non‐CKD kidney conditions (e.g. isolated nephrolithiasis or urinary tract infections). Types of interventions We plan to evaluate the following treatment comparisons. Any pharmacological interventions, including but not limited to antiviral agents, neutralising monoclonal antibodies, IL inhibitors, anti‐inflammatory drugs, immunomodulators, and antimalarial drugs versus placebo. Any pharmacological interventions versus standard care or no treatment. Any pharmacological interventions versus other pharmacological interventions (e.g. neutralising monoclonal antibodies, IL inhibitors, immunomodulators, and antimalarial drugs). The same pharmacological intervention delivered at different doses, frequencies, durations, or routes of administration (e.g. high‐dose versus low‐dose corticosteroids, intravenous versus oral administration). We will evaluate interventions delivered by any route (e.g. oral, intravenous, or subcutaneous) at any dose, frequency, or duration. Outcome measures We will not exclude studies based on non‐reporting of outcomes of interest. The outcomes selected include the relevant core outcome sets developed by the Standardised Outcomes in Nephrology (SONG) initiative, including the general SONG COVID‐19 core outcome set [ 25 ], and the disease‐specific sets: SONG‐HD [ 26 ], SONG‐PD [ 27 ], and SONG‐Tx (kidney transplantation) [ 28 ], as well as the core outcome sets for CKD recommended by the KDIGO guidelines [ 24 ]. Critical outcomes Death (any cause): death from any cause during follow‐up. For acute COVID‐19 outcomes, the longest follow‐up within 30 days will be prioritised. Respiratory failure: requirement for invasive mechanical ventilation or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation during hospitalisation. Assessed at the longest follow‐up within 30 days. Cardiovascular composite outcome: major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), defined as a composite of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke, or hospitalisation for heart failure, as defined by study authors. Kidney function decline or AKI, a composite of: New or worsening AKI (as defined by study authors, including KDIGO criteria where available); ≥ 30% decline in eGFR; Initiation of KRT. Life participation: assessed using validated patient‐reported outcome measures reflecting the ability to engage in usual life activities, work, and social participation at the longest available follow‐up. Important outcomes Serious adverse events: defined by study authors or regulatory definitions. Hospital length of stay: duration of hospitalisation in days. Thromboembolic events: venous or arterial thromboembolic events during follow‐up. For acute outcomes (death, respiratory failure, cardiovascular events), we will prioritise the longest reported follow‐up within 30 days. For kidney‐related and life participation outcomes, we will use the longest available follow‐up reported by the study authors. Where multiple measurement instruments are used, validated instruments will be prioritised. Search methods for identification of studies Electronic searches The Cochrane Kidney and Transplant Information Specialist will search the following databases for RCTs without language, publication year or publication status restrictions. Cochrane Kidney and Transplant Specialised Register via MeerKat (a software application built on Microsoft Access® used to manage the database). MeerKat is a study‐based register and is used to store bibliographic and study details, link multiple reports to a single study, link studies to reviews, and track the progress of reviews. Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) via the Cochrane Library (latest issue). Ovid MEDLINE® ALL (from 1946). Embase.com records as part of the search of CENTRAL as described in How CENTRAL is created ( https://www.cochranelibrary.com/central/central-creation ). US National Institutes of Health Ongoing Trials Register ClinicalTrials.gov ( https://www.clinicaltrials.gov ) as part of the search of CENTRAL. World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform ( https://trialsearch.who.int ) as part of the search of CENTRAL. The Information Specialist will model the subject strategies for other databases on the search strategy designed for MEDLINE. MEDLINE searches will combine the subject strategy adaptations with the sensitivity‐ and precision‐maximising search strategy designed by Cochrane for identifying RCTs, as described in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions (version 5.1.0), and updated to account for new MeSH study types and wider use of machine indexing by the National Library of Medicine (NLM) [ 29 ]. Please see Supplementary material 1 for the search terms used. Searching other resources We will check the reference lists of included studies and any relevant systematic reviews identified for further references to relevant studies. We will check the included studies for retractions and errata via the Retraction Watch Database and report the search dates in the review ( https://retractiondatabase.org ). We will search Epistemonikos for related systematic reviews ( https://www.epistemonikos.org ). We may contact the original authors or funders of included studies for clarification and further data if study reports are unclear. Data collection and analysis Selection of studies The search strategy described will be used to obtain titles and abstracts of studies that may be relevant to the review. The titles and abstracts will be screened independently by two review authors (SA, KH), who will discard studies that are not applicable; however, studies and reviews that might include relevant data or information on studies will be retained initially. Two review authors (SA, KH) will independently assess retrieved abstracts and, if necessary, the full text of these studies to determine which studies satisfy the inclusion criteria. The discrepancies will be solved by consultation with a third review author (PN). If the number of records identified is substantial, additional trained reviewers will be recruited to support screening and data extraction to ensure feasibility and methodological rigour. Data extraction and management Data extraction will be carried out independently by two review authors (SA, KH) using standard data extraction forms. Studies reported in non‐English language journals will be translated before assessment, as possible. Where more than one publication of one study exists, reports will be grouped together and the publication with the most complete data will be used in the analysis. Where relevant outcomes are only published in earlier versions, these data will be used. Any discrepancies between published versions will be highlighted. From each study, we will extract the following information: authors, year of publication, country, language, setting (single centre or multicentre), study design, number of participants, age, gender, stage of CKD, comorbidities, severity of COVID‐19 at baseline, time from symptom onset to treatment initiation, SARS‐CoV‐2 variant or strain, COVID‐19 vaccination status, types of intervention, dose, route, frequency, follow‐up, and critical and important outcomes. Any discrepancies will be resolved by consultation with a third review author (PN). Risk of bias assessment in included studies The following items will be independently assessed for each outcome by three authors (SA, KH, PN) using the Cochrane risk of bias 2 (RoB 2) tool [ 30 ] (available at https://www.riskofbias.info/ ). This tool evaluates the risk of bias across five domains. Bias arising from the randomisation process Bias due to deviations from intended interventions Including whether the trial was analysed according to the assigned intervention (intention‐to‐treat (ITT)) Bias due to missing outcome data Bias in the measurement of the outcome Bias in the selection of the reported result. Each outcome domain will be judged as "low risk," "some concerns," or "high risk" of bias, and an overall risk of bias judgement will be assigned for each outcome. We will conduct RoB 2 assessments for the outcomes included in the summary of findings tables at the prespecified prioritised time points. For cluster‐RCTs, we will use the RoB 2 extension for cluster designs. Additional domains will include bias arising from the recruitment of participants within clusters, baseline imbalances, loss of clusters, and incorrect analysis that does not account for clustering. The discrepancies will be solved by consultation with a third review author (PN). Measures of treatment effect For dichotomous outcomes, we will calculate risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). For continuous outcomes, we will calculate mean differences (MD) or standardised mean differences (SMD) with 95% CI. For time‐to‐event outcomes, we will use hazard ratios (HR) and pool data using the generic inverse variance method where appropriate. Where studies report medians and interquartile ranges, we will convert these to means and standard deviations (SD) using methods described in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 31 ]. The following measurement tools may be used across studies. Kidney function : eGFR, serum creatinine (SCr), or creatinine clearance (CrCl). Lung function : Forced Expiratory Volume in 1 second (FEV₁), Diffusing Capacity of the Lung for Carbon Monoxide (DLCO), oxygen saturation, or residual volume. Fatigue : Fatigue Severity Scale (FSS) [ 32 ], visual analogue scales (VAS) [ 33 ], or other validated patient‐reported measures. Health‐related quality of life (HRQoL) : EuroQol 5 Dimension (EQ‐5D) [ 34 ], Short Form 36 question survey (SF‐36) [ 35 ], or disease‐specific tools like Kidney Disease Quality of Life short form (KDQOL‐SF) [ 36 ]. Life participation : SONG life participation instrument [ 37 ]. Where only medians and interquartile ranges are reported, we will convert these to means and SDs using established methods where appropriate. If data are only available in graphical form, we will attempt to extract values using validated digital tools or by contacting the study authors for clarification. Unit of analysis issues Cluster‐randomised studies We anticipate that studies using cluster randomisation will have been controlled for clustering effects. In case of doubt, we will contact the authors and request individual participant data to calculate an estimate of the intra‐cluster correlation coefficient (ICC). If this is not possible, we will obtain external estimates of the ICC from a similar study or from a study of a similar population as described in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 31 ]. When the ICC is established, we will use it to re‐analyse the study data. If ICCs from other sources are used, we will report this and conduct sensitivity analyses to investigate the effect of variation in the ICC. Cross‐over studies Cross‐over studies will be analysed using only the outcomes reported in the first period, as available. Studies with more than two treatment arms For studies with more than two treatment arms, we will include all relevant arms that meet the inclusion criteria. If multiple active treatment arms are reported, we will: Combine similar intervention groups (e.g. two doses of the same drug) when clinically appropriate to allow for a single pair‐wise comparison. If combining is not appropriate, we will compare each relevant intervention arm separately with the control group, adjusting for the shared comparator group as recommended in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions (e.g. by splitting the control group’s sample size across comparisons to avoid double‐counting) [ 31 ]. We will document and justify any such decisions transparently. Dealing with missing data Any additional information required from the original authors will be requested by written correspondence (e.g. emailing the corresponding author), and any relevant information obtained will be included in the review. Evaluation of important numerical data such as screened and randomised people as well as ITT, as‐treated and per‐protocol populations, will be performed. Attrition rates (including dropouts, losses to follow‐up, and withdrawals) will be investigated. Issues of missing data and imputation methods (e.g. last‐observation‐carried‐forward) will be critically appraised. The primary analysis will use ITT data where available. Per‐protocol and as‐treated analyses will be examined in sensitivity analyses to assess the robustness of findings to missing data and protocol deviations. Reporting bias assessment When 10 or more studies report outcomes, funnel plots will be used to assess potential small study bias [ 38 ]. If asymmetry is evident, we will investigate publication bias using Egger’s test. We will review all clinical trials registries and published protocols to assess potential reporting biases of the included RCTs. Synthesis methods We will use a random‐effects model as clinical and methodological heterogeneity is expected. The Restricted Maximum Likelihood (REML) estimator will be used to estimate between‐study variance [ 39 ]. The Hartung–Knapp–Sidik–Jonkman method will be applied when there are at least three studies, and heterogeneity is present. In other situations, a Wald‐type method will be used [ 40 ]. A fixed‐effect model will be used in sensitivity analyses. Investigation of heterogeneity and subgroup analysis We will assess heterogeneity among studies using the Chi² test (with a significance level of P < 0.10) and quantify inconsistency using the I² statistic. An I² value of 30% to 60% may represent moderate heterogeneity, 50% to 90% substantial heterogeneity, and greater than 75% considerable heterogeneity. Where sufficient data are available, we will conduct subgroup analyses to explore potential sources of heterogeneity. Age group (e.g. children versus adults; older versus younger adults) Sex Timing of initiation of treatment (early versus late treatment, as defined by study authors) Year of recruitment (reflecting pandemic waves) Dominant viral variant (where reported) Vaccination availability (pre‐vaccination versus post‐vaccination era). Subgroup analyses will be conducted by stratifying studies according to these characteristics and comparing pooled effect estimates across subgroups. We will use interaction tests to compare subgroups in Review Manager (RevMan) [ 41 ]. Subgroup findings will be interpreted with caution due to potential residual confounding and multiple testing. Equity‐related assessment We will consider equity‐related issues in accordance with the PROGRESS‐Plus framework (Place of residence, Race/ethnicity, Occupation, Gender/sex, Religion, Education, Socioeconomic status, Social capital, plus additional context‐specific factors) [ 42 ]. Based on clinical and contextual relevance to CKD and COVID‐19, we have prespecified the following equity‐related characteristics for subgroup analyses. Country income level (low‐ and middle‐income countries versus high‐income countries) Age group Sex Vaccination status. Where sufficient data are available, we will explore whether treatment effects differ across these groups. We will also provide a narrative commentary on the representation of disadvantaged or underrepresented populations in the included studies and the potential implications for the applicability and generalisability of the findings. Sensitivity analysis We will perform sensitivity analyses to assess the robustness of the findings to key methodological decisions and assumptions. The following sensitivity analyses are planned. Risk of bias – excluding studies judged to be at high risk of bias to assess the impact of study limitations on effect estimates. Statistical model – comparing results obtained using fixed‐effect and random‐effects models to examine the influence of model choice. Imputed or missing data – excluding studies with substantial missing outcome data or where imputation methods were applied, to assess the impact of assumptions regarding missing data. Cluster‐RCTs (ICC assumptions) – where cluster‐randomised trials do not report an ICC and an ICC is imputed, we will conduct sensitivity analyses using a range of plausible ICC values to examine the impact of this assumption. Borderline eligibility decisions – where inclusion required judgement (e.g. unclear CKD definition or mixed populations), we will explore the effect of excluding such studies. These analyses are intended to evaluate the stability and reliability of the primary findings. Certainty of the evidence assessment We will assess the certainty of the evidence for each critical and important outcome using the GRADE approach [ 43 , 44 , 45 ]. The GRADE approach defines the certainty of a body of evidence as the extent to which one can be confident that an estimate of effect or association is close to the true quantity of specific interest. The certainty of a body of evidence involves consideration of within‐trial risk of bias (methodological quality), directness of evidence, heterogeneity, precision of effect estimates, and risk of publication bias. The overall certainty of evidence for each outcome will be graded as high, moderate, low, or very low. Three review authors (SA, KH, PN) will independently assess certainty and resolve disagreements through discussion or consultation with a fourth reviewer. We will prepare one summary of findings (SoF) table per intervention comparison. Specifically, we will present separate SoF tables for (1) any pharmacological intervention versus placebo and (2) any pharmacological intervention versus standard care or no treatment. The primary comparison will be intervention versus placebo or standard care. The SoF tables will include the following critical outcomes assessed at the prioritised time points defined above. Death (any cause) Respiratory failure Cardiovascular composite outcome Kidney function decline or AKI composite Life participation. Consumer involvement Consumers were not involved in the development of this protocol due to lack of dedicated resources and infrastructure to support meaningful engagement at this stage. To enhance relevance, we prioritised patient‐important outcomes identified by the SONG initiative and simplified technical terminology. A plain language summary will be developed at the full review stage in accordance with Cochrane guidelines for language and accessibility. documents.title: Exercise training for adults with chronic kidney disease not requiring dialysis.
documents.abstract: OBJECTIVES: This is a protocol for a Cochrane Review (intervention). The objectives are as follows: To evaluate the benefits and harms of regular, structured exercise training in adults with chronic kidney disease not requiring dialysis, focusing on patient-important outcomes such as death, cardiovascular events, fatigue, functional capacity, and depression.

Objectives This is a protocol for a Cochrane Review (intervention). The objectives are as follows: To evaluate the benefits and harms of regular, structured exercise training in adults with chronic kidney disease not requiring dialysis, focusing on patient‐important outcomes such as death, cardiovascular events, fatigue, functional capacity, and depression. status released display-pdf yes is-olf no is-manuscript no is-preprint no is-journal-matter no is-scanned no is-retracted no Collection date 2026. Background Regular physical activity is a cornerstone of health promotion and cardiovascular disease prevention. Although individuals with chronic kidney disease (CKD) are at markedly increased risk of cardiovascular morbidity and death [ 1 ], they often have a reduced capacity to engage in physical exercise [ 2 ]. This reduced capacity is thought to result from a combination of CKD‐related factors, including hormonal and immune dysregulation, muscle wasting, anaemia, and impaired oxygen utilisation [ 3 , 4 ]. Description of the condition CKD is defined as persistent abnormalities in kidney structure or function lasting at least three months, with potential implications for overall health [ 5 ]. CKD is classified based on its underlying cause, level of glomerular filtration rate (GFR), and degree of albuminuria. In its most advanced stage—kidney failure—patients typically require kidney replacement therapy (KRT), such as haemodialysis (HD), peritoneal dialysis (PD), or kidney transplantation. Description of the intervention and how it might work Physical activity encompasses a range of modalities that vary in type, intensity, frequency, and duration. Aerobic (or cardiovascular) exercise increases heart and respiratory rates, such as running, cycling, walking, or swimming. Resistance exercise focuses on enhancing muscle strength, tone, and mass through activities like lifting weights or using resistance bands. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that adults aged 18 to 64 engage in at least 150 minutes of moderate‐intensity or 75 minutes of vigorous‐intensity aerobic activity per week to promote cardiovascular and muscular fitness [ 6 ]. In line with evidence from the general population, the 2024 KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of Chronic Kidney Disease encourages individuals with CKD to be as physically active as their cardiovascular status and tolerance permit, aiming for 150 minutes of activity per week [ 5 ]. Exercise training holds promise for improving a wide range of outcomes in people with CKD. In the general population, regular physical activity is associated with lower risks of death (any cause), coronary heart disease, hypertension, stroke, type 2 diabetes, metabolic syndrome, and certain cancers [ 6 ]. Additionally, exercise has been shown to alleviate fatigue in patients with cancer [ 7 ] and chronic fatigue syndrome [ 8 ]. By improving cardiovascular endurance and muscle strength, exercise may enhance both health outcomes and day‐to‐day functioning in this population. Why it is important to do this review Patients, caregivers, and healthcare professionals consistently identify lifestyle interventions—particularly exercise—as a top research priority in CKD [ 9 , 10 ]. Despite this, most randomised controlled trials (RCTs) in CKD fail to align with patient priorities or focus on patient‐important outcomes [ 11 ]. A prior Cochrane review concluded that exercise training may improve physical fitness, health‐related quality of life (HRQoL), and certain cardiovascular and nutritional parameters [ 12 ]. However, the certainty of the evidence was low, and critical outcomes such as death, cardiovascular events, and fatigue were not adequately assessed. Although numerous studies have been published since, there remains no clear consensus on the effectiveness or safety of exercise interventions in adults receiving maintenance dialysis. Objectives To evaluate the benefits and harms of regular, structured exercise training in adults with chronic kidney disease not requiring dialysis, focusing on patient‐important outcomes such as death, cardiovascular events, fatigue, functional capacity, and depression. Methods Criteria for considering studies for this review Types of studies We will include only RCTs that evaluate a structured programme of regular physical exercise in adults with CKD who do not require dialysis. All variants of RCT design will be eligible, including parallel‐group, cross‐over, cluster‐RCTs, stepped‐wedge, factorial, and multi‐arm trials, provided that at least one eligible comparison (exercise versus no structured exercise) can be extracted. We will exclude quasi‐RCTs, non‐randomised, observational, and pre‐post studies without a control group. Types of participants We will include studies involving adults with CKD at any stage (1–5) who are not receiving KRT (HD, PD, or kidney transplantation). This includes participants with CKD stage 5 who have not yet initiated dialysis. We will perform sensitivity analyses to explore whether inclusion of this subgroup influences results, given potential clinical heterogeneity. We will exclude studies of adults undergoing maintenance dialysis because exercise interventions in that population are typically delivered during dialysis and represent a distinct intervention type that has been evaluated in a separate Cochrane review [ 12 ]. Studies of adults with acute kidney injury, kidney transplant recipients, or paediatric populations will also be excluded. If a study includes a broader population in which only a subset of participants meets the review’s eligibility criteria (e.g. a mixed CKD and dialysis population), we will include the study only if outcome data for the eligible subgroup are available. When subgroup data are not presented separately, we will contact study authors to request disaggregated results. If subgroup data remain unavailable, the study will be excluded from quantitative synthesis but may be described narratively if relevant. All decisions regarding partial inclusion or exclusion will be documented transparently. Types of interventions Interventions We will include interventions consisting of a structured programme of regular physical exercise designed to improve or maintain general fitness and functional capacity. A structured programme is defined as a planned, repetitive, and purposeful series of physical activities with a clearly described type, frequency, intensity, and duration. To be eligible, interventions must: Include an exercise component of at least eight weeks’ duration and a minimum frequency of one session per week; Target overall physical conditioning (e.g. aerobic capacity, muscular strength, endurance, balance, or flexibility); Provide sufficient detail to allow replication (type of activity, session length, and progression over time). Delivery and supervision Exercise training may be delivered individually or in groups, in‐person or remotely (e.g. home‐based or digital), and may be self‐managed or supervised by a healthcare or exercise professional (e.g. physiotherapist, exercise physiologist, nurse, or researcher). We will extract and analyse details of delivery setting (hospital, rehabilitation centre, community gym, or home), supervision level, and whether the intervention was tailored or standardised. Comparators Eligible comparators include usual care, attention control, or sham interventions (e.g. light stretching without aerobic or resistance training). Studies that only promote or recommend physical activity without a structured exercise component will be excluded. Interventions targeting a single muscle group for purposes unrelated to general fitness (e.g. respiratory muscle training or hand–forearm exercise for vascular access maturation) will also be excluded. Outcome measures We will focus on outcomes identified as important by patients and caregivers through the Standardised Outcomes in Nephrology‐Chronic Kidney Disease (SONG‐CKD) initiative [ 13 ]. Each outcome will be extracted for the prespecified primary time point of interest (end of the intervention or longest available follow‐up, as detailed below). Critical outcomes Death (any cause): number of deaths from any cause at the longest available follow‐up. Cardiovascular events: composite or individual major adverse cardiovascular events (e.g. myocardial infarction, stroke, sudden cardiac death, coronary revascularisation, hospitalisation for heart failure) at the longest follow‐up. Progression of CKD: initiation of KRT, sustained decline in estimated (e) GFR (≥ 30% or ≥ 40% from baseline), doubling of serum creatinine, or eGFR < 15 mL/min/1.73 m², assessed at the longest follow‐up. Important outcomes HRQoL: measured using validated instruments such as Short Form 36 question survey (SF‐36), Kidney Disease Quality of Life (KDQOL), EuroQol 5 Dimension (EQ‐5D), or similar; assessed at the end of the intervention. Fatigue: assessed using validated scales such as Functional Assessment of Chronic Illness Therapy‐Fatigue (FACIT‐Fatigue) or the Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory (MFI‐20); measured at the end of the intervention. Physical function: objective performance tests including the 6‐minute walk test (6MWT), sit‐to‐stand test, timed up‐and‐go, handgrip strength, or Short Physical Performance Battery; measured at the end of the intervention. Depressive symptoms: measured using validated instruments such as the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI) or Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ‐9); measured at the end of intervention. Blood pressure: mean change in resting systolic (SBP) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) (mmHg) at the end of the intervention. Adverse events related to exercise: any event considered related to the intervention (e.g. musculoskeletal injury, cardiovascular symptoms, or withdrawal due to adverse effects) reported during the intervention period. If multiple time points are reported, we will use the end‐of‐intervention measurement for functional and patient‐reported outcomes, and the longest follow‐up for death, cardiovascular events, and CKD progression. Units and scales will be extracted as reported and standardised for meta‐analysis when appropriate. Search methods for identification of studies Electronic searches The Cochrane Kidney and Transplant Information Specialist will search the following databases for RCTs without language, publication year or publication status restrictions. Cochrane Kidney and Transplant Specialised Register via MeerKat (a software application built on Microsoft Access used to manage the database). MeerKat is a study‐based register and is used to store bibliographic and study details, link multiple reports to a single study, link studies to reviews, and track the progress of reviews. Ovid MEDLINE® ALL (from 1946) Ovid Embase (the last 12 months) Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) via the Cochrane Library Embase.com records as part of the search of CENTRAL, as described in 'How CENTRAL is created' ( https://www.cochranelibrary.com/central/central-creation ) US National Institutes of Health Ongoing Trials Register ClinicalTrials.gov ( https://www.clinicaltrials.gov ) as part of the search of CENTRAL WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform ( https://trialsearch.who.int ) as part of the search of CENTRAL. The Information Specialist will model the subject strategies for other databases on the search strategy designed for MEDLINE. MEDLINE searches combine the subject strategy adaptations with the Sensitivity and precision maximising search strategy designed by Cochrane for identifying RCTs (as described in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions Version 5.1.0) and updated by us to account for new MeSH study types and wider use of machine indexing by the National Library of Medicine (NLM) [ 14 ]. Additional search strategies have been designed by the Information Specialist for MEDLINE, Embase and CENTRAL. We present the search strategies in Supplementary material 1 . Searching other resources We will check the reference lists of included studies and any relevant systematic reviews identified for further references to relevant studies. We will check the included studies for retractions and errata via the Retraction Watch Database and report the search dates in the review ( https://retractiondatabase.org ). We will search Epistemonikos for related systematic reviews ( https://www.epistemonikos.org ). We may contact the original authors or funders of included studies for clarification and further data if study reports are unclear. Data collection and analysis Selection of studies The search strategy will be used to identify titles and abstracts of potentially relevant studies. Two review authors will independently screen these records, excluding studies that do not meet the inclusion criteria. However, studies and reviews that may contain relevant data or information on eligible studies will be retained at this stage. Two review authors will independently assess the full texts of potentially eligible studies to determine final inclusion. Any disagreements will be resolved through discussion or consultation with a third review author. None of the review authors have authored or are directly involved in any studies that are potentially eligible for inclusion in this review. Therefore, no conflict‐of‐interest management procedures related to study authorship are required. Data extraction and management At least two review authors will independently extract both study characteristics and outcome data from each included study using a standardised and piloted Excel spreadsheet developed for this review. The spreadsheet will capture all study characteristics, participant details, interventions, comparators, and outcomes described below. Any disagreements between review authors during data extraction will be resolved through discussion and consensus; if consensus cannot be reached, a third review author will arbitrate. When clarification is required to determine study eligibility or to obtain missing or unclear data, we will contact study authors by email, with up to two follow‐up attempts spaced at least two weeks apart. If no response is received, we will base our assessment on the available data and document the uncertainty. All correspondence with study authors will be logged and summarised in the review. We will extract the following data items. Study identification and general information Trial name and registration number Corresponding author contact information Study aim or objective Year and language of publication Source of funding Trial start and end dates. Study setting and design Country or countries where the study was conducted Single‐centre or multi‐centre design Type of healthcare facility (e.g. hospital, outpatient clinic) Study design (e.g. parallel RCT) Total number of participants randomised to intervention and control groups Duration of follow‐up Recruitment methods Whether the study was powered for a specific outcome Whether informed consent was obtained Ethics committee approval. Participant characteristics Inclusion and exclusion criteria Baseline characteristics: age, sex, body mass index (BMI), eGFR, diabetes status, hypertension status, and CKD stage according to 2024 KDIGO guidelines [ 5 ]. Intervention details Type and description of the exercise intervention Equipment or materials used Frequency and duration of training sessions Supervision (supervised versus unsupervised) Mode of delivery (e.g. in‐person, home‐based, digital) Setting of the intervention (e.g. hospital, gym, home) Target exercise intensity Whether the intervention was tailored or standardised across participants Whether the duration or intensity progressed over time Measures of adherence (e.g. session attendance, percentage completion) Description of any co‐interventions. Comparator or control Description and nature of the comparator (e.g. usual care, sham intervention, no intervention) Outcome measures We will extract data on the predefined patient‐important outcomes, following the SONG‐CKD core outcome set for adults with CKD [ 13 ]. Dichotomous outcomes: death (any cause), cardiovascular events, CKD progression, and adverse events Number of events and total number of participants in each group Continuous outcomes: HRQoL, fatigue, physical function, depressive symptoms, blood pressure Change from baseline and standard deviation (SD) Post‐intervention means and SDs If SDs are not available, standard errors (SEs) or 95% confidence intervals (CIs) will be extracted and converted to SDs where appropriate. Risk of bias assessment in included studies At least two review authors will work independently to assess risk of bias for each included study using the Cochrane Risk of Bias (RoB) version 1 tool [ 15 ] (see Supplementary material 2 ). Any disagreements will be resolved through discussion and consensus; if consensus cannot be reached, a third reviewer will arbitrate. Was there adequate sequence generation (selection bias)? Was allocation adequately concealed (selection bias)? Was knowledge of the allocated interventions adequately prevented during the study? Participants and personnel (performance bias) Outcome assessors (detection bias) Were incomplete outcome data adequately addressed (attrition bias)? Are reports of the study free of suggestion of selective outcome reporting (reporting bias)? Was the study apparently free of other problems that could put it at risk of bias? For cluster RCTs, issues specific to the design will be assessed within the'Other bias' domain. These may include recruitment bias, baseline imbalances between clusters, loss or exclusion of entire clusters after randomisation, and whether the analysis appropriately accounted for clustering. We will also consider whether features of the cluster design limit comparability with individual RCTs. All such considerations will be described narratively and incorporated into the overall RoB judgement for each cluster‐RCT, and reflected within the 'Other bias' domain. Measures of treatment effect For dichotomous outcomes, we will calculate risk ratios (RRs) with 95% CIs. For continuous outcomes, we will calculate the mean differences (MD) with 95% CIs. When studies use different scales to measure the same construct, we will use standardised mean difference (SMD) with 95% CIs. If studies report both change‐from‐baseline and post‐intervention values, we will preferentially use change scores when baseline imbalance is possible; otherwise, we will use post‐intervention data. For count data (e.g. number of cardiovascular events, hospitalisations, or adverse events per participant), we will extract and analyse rate data as rate ratios when person‐time is reported. If person‐time data are unavailable and only the total number of events per group is provided, we will treat the outcome as dichotomous (participants with ≥ 1 event versus none) and conduct sensitivity analyses to explore the impact of this assumption. When studies report skewed data or results are reported as medians and interquartile ranges (IQR), we will estimate means and SDs using established conversion methods [ 16 , 17 ]. Where possible, we will interpret treatment effects relative to minimal clinically important differences (MCIDs) or thresholds for clinical significance established in related populations. Unit of analysis issues This review will include only RCTs that evaluate a structured programme of regular physical exercise in adults with CKD not requiring dialysis. All variants of RCT design will be eligible, including parallel‐group, cross‐over, cluster RCTs, stepped‐wedge, factorial, and multi‐arm trials, provided that at least one eligible comparison (exercise versus no structured exercise) can be extracted. Cross‐over trials: Given the potential for carry‐over effects from exercise interventions, we will include only data from the first treatment period (assuming random allocation at baseline) and will treat the study as a parallel‐group trial. Cluster RCTs: To account for the unit‐of‐analysis error that arises from clustering, we will adjust the effective sample size using the design effect, calculated as: Design effect = 1 + ρ (M − 1), where ρ is the intra‐cluster correlation coefficient (ICC), and M is the average cluster size. If the ICC is not reported, we will use external estimates from similar studies or conduct sensitivity analyses using a range of plausible ICCs. Stepped‐wedge trials: We will extract outcome data from the latest time point before the final cluster receives the intervention, treating clusters that have not yet received the intervention as controls. Factorial trials: When only one comparison is relevant to this review, we will analyse the full marginal comparison for that factor, including all participants regardless of the other intervention. If more than one factor is relevant, we will include each relevant marginal comparison in the meta‐analysis as a separate comparison. We will check whether important interactions between interventions have been reported and consider this in the interpretation of results. Multi‐arm trials: When multiple intervention arms meet inclusion criteria (e.g. aerobic and resistance training), we will combine these arms for the main analysis to avoid double‐counting participants. If arms belong to different subgroups but share a single control group, we will divide the control group sample size evenly across comparisons. Repeated measures within participants: For studies reporting multiple outcome measurements per participant (e.g. at multiple time points during the intervention), we will extract data at the prespecified time point of interest (the end of the intervention for functional and symptom outcomes, and the longest follow‐up for clinical outcomes). If a study reports several relevant outcomes on the same construct (e.g. multiple physical function tests), we will select the most commonly reported or clinically relevant measure to avoid multiple comparisons within the same population. In all analyses, we will ensure that no participant is included more than once within a single meta‐analysis comparison. Dealing with missing data We will attempt to obtain missing or incomplete data by contacting the study authors via email or other written correspondence. This includes situations where: Essential outcome data are not reported in the published manuscript; Only abstract results are available and no corresponding full‐text publication can be identified; There is uncertainty regarding whether a publication represents a secondary analysis or a duplicate report of an included study. In cases where outcome data are presented only in graphical format, we will extract numerical estimates using digital data extraction tools (e.g. WebPlotDigitizer) to the best of our ability. These estimates will be used in the meta‐analysis and clearly flagged as extracted data. For continuous outcomes reported as medians with ranges or IQRs, we will estimate means and SDs using established methods such as those described by Wan and coauthors [ 17 ] or Luo and coauthors [ 16 ], depending on the summary statistics provided. If SDs are not reported and cannot be calculated, we will impute the missing SD using the largest reported SD from other included studies that contribute to the same meta‐analysis. Sensitivity analyses will be conducted to assess the impact of these imputations on the overall results. All imputed or estimated values will be clearly documented, and assumptions will be tested in sensitivity analyses when appropriate. Reporting bias assessment For meta‐analyses that include 10 or more studies, we will generate funnel plots to visually assess asymmetry. Where appropriate, we will apply statistical tests for funnel plot asymmetry, such as Egger’s test for continuous outcomes and Harbord’s test for binary outcomes, while recognising their limitations in the presence of substantial heterogeneity or small numbers of studies [ 18 ]. In addition, we will assess for selective outcome reporting by comparing reported outcomes with those pre‐specified in study protocols or trial registry entries, when available. Discrepancies will be documented and considered in the risk of bias assessment. Synthesis methods The primary comparison of interest will be structured exercise training versus no structured exercise (e.g. usual care, attention control, or sham exercise). If sufficient data are available, we will conduct separate meta‐analyses for specific exercise modalities (aerobic, resistance, or combined training) compared with no structured exercise. We expect clinical diversity among studies; therefore, we will use a random‐effects model for all meta‐analyses. Between‐study variance (τ²) will be estimated using the Restricted Maximum Likelihood (REML) method [ 19 ]. The Hartung‐Knapp‐Sidik‐Jonkman adjustment will be applied to calculate confidence intervals when there are at least three studies and the estimated heterogeneity is greater than zero [ 20 ]. In other situations (e.g. only two studies or τ² = 0), we will use the Wald‐type method. We will report τ² estimates and 95 % prediction intervals for each meta‐analysis. We will also perform fixed‐effect sensitivity analyses to assess the influence of the statistical model on pooled results. Separate meta‐analyses will be conducted for dichotomous and continuous outcomes using RRs and MD (or SMD), respectively. Investigation of heterogeneity and subgroup analysis We will first assess heterogeneity by visual inspection of forest plots. Statistical heterogeneity will be quantified using the I² statistic, which describes the percentage of total variation across studies that is due to heterogeneity rather than chance. As a guide to interpretation: 0% to 40%: might not be important; 30% to 60%: may represent moderate heterogeneity; 50% to 90%: may represent substantial heterogeneity; 75% to 100%: considerable heterogeneity. The importance of the observed I² value will depend on the magnitude and direction of effects and on the number of studies included. We will conduct subgroup analyses to explore potential sources of heterogeneity when sufficient data are available (e.g. ≥ 10 studies per comparison). Planned subgroups Type of exercise: aerobic versus resistance versus combined aerobic and resistance training. Duration of intervention: four months or less versus more than four months. In our Cochrane review of exercise training in adults receiving maintenance dialysis [ 12 ], improvements in depressive symptoms were seen only in interventions lasting more than four months. This cut‐off will help determine whether longer training durations yield greater benefits. Exercise intensity: light to moderate versus moderate to vigorous (as defined by study authors). Supervision: supervised versus unsupervised/home‐based programmes. We will assess subgroup effects using the formal Test for Subgroup Differences in RevMan to evaluate whether observed differences between subgroups are statistically significant. Subgroup analyses will be interpreted as exploratory and hypothesis‐generating. Equity‐related assessment We will assess whether included studies report equity‐related characteristics using the PROGRESS‐Plus framework (Place of residence, Race/ethnicity/culture/language, Occupation, Gender or sex, Religion, Education, Socioeconomic status, and Social capital, plus personal characteristics, relationships, and time‐dependent factors) [ 21 ]. For this review, factors most likely to be relevant to exercise interventions in CKD include sex, age, comorbidity burden (e.g. hypertension or diabetes), and underlying cause of CKD. Where such data are reported, we will describe them narratively and, if feasible, explore whether these factors modify the effects of exercise interventions. Sensitivity analysis We will conduct sensitivity analyses to assess the robustness of our findings and to determine whether key methodological decisions or assumptions influence results. Specifically, we will perform the following sensitivity analyses where data allow. Excluding studies assessed as having a high risk of bias Using alternative statistical models (i.e. fixed‐effect versus random‐effects models) Excluding studies with imputed or estimated data (e.g. imputed SDs) Excluding unpublished studies or those published only as abstracts. We will compare the results of these analyses to the primary meta‐analyses and assess the impact on overall effect estimates and CIs. Any material differences in results will be documented and considered when interpreting the certainty of evidence. Certainty of the evidence assessment We will assess the certainty of the evidence for each outcome using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach, evaluating risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias. Two review authors will independently assess the certainty of the body of evidence for each outcome. Any disagreements will be resolved through discussion or, if needed, by consultation with a third review author. A summary of findings (SoF) table will be prepared using GRADEpro GDT [ 22 ] for the main comparison of structured exercise training versus no structured exercise (usual care or sham exercise). The table will present the following outcomes, measures, and primary time points. Outcome Measure Primary time point Death (any cause) RR Longest available follow‐up Cardiovascular events RR Longest available follow‐up Progression of CKD RR Longest available follow‐up HRQoL MD or SMD (validated scales such as SF‐36, KDQOL, or EQ‐5D) End of intervention Fatigue MD or SMD (FACIT‐F or MFI‐20) End of intervention Physical function MD or SMD (e.g. 6MWT, sit‐to‐stand, or handgrip strength) End of intervention Adverse events related to exercise RR During intervention Consumer involvement This review prioritises outcomes identified as important by patients and caregivers through the SONG‐CKD initiative [ 13 ], ensuring the focus remains on issues that matter most to people living with CKD. Patients and consumers will be involved in reviewing draft materials to ensure the content is clear, relevant, and accessible to lay audiences. Supplementary material 3 describes the planned consumer involvement in more detail, including how patient and caregiver perspectives will inform interpretation of findings and dissemination of results. documents.title: Metformin for preventing the progression of chronic kidney disease.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Metformin has been used in the management of diabetes for decades. It is an effective, low-cost intervention with a well-established safety profile. Emerging evidence suggests that metformin targets a number of pathways that lead to chronic kidney damage, and long-term use may, therefore, slow the rate of kidney function decline and chronic kidney disease (CKD) progression.
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the effect of metformin therapy on kidney function decline in patients with CKD with or without diabetes mellitus and assess the safety and dose tolerability in this population.
SEARCH METHODS: We searched the Cochrane Kidney and Transplant Register of Studies up to 19 July 2023 with assistance from an Information Specialist using search terms relevant to this review. Studies in the Register are identified through searches of CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, conference proceedings, the International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP) Search Portal and ClinicalTrials.gov.
SELECTION CRITERIA: We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) that reported kidney-related outcomes with a minimum duration of 12 months delivery of the metformin intervention and whose eligibility criteria included adult participants with either i) a diagnosis of CKD of any aetiology and/or ii) those with a diagnosis of diabetes mellitus. Comparisons included placebo, no intervention, non-pharmacological interventions, other antidiabetic medications or any other active control. Studies that included patients on any modality of kidney replacement therapy were excluded.
DATA COLLECTION AND ANALYSIS: Two authors independently carried out data extraction using a standard data extraction form. The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed using the Cochrane risk of bias tool. Summary estimates of effect were obtained using a random-effects model, and results were expressed as risk ratios (RR) and their 95% confidence intervals (CI) for dichotomous outcomes and mean difference (MD) and 95% CI for continuous outcomes. Confidence in the evidence was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach.
MAIN RESULTS: This review included 11 studies reporting on 8449 randomised participants. Studies were conducted in patient populations with Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD) (four studies) or diabetes mellitus (seven studies). Six studies compared metformin with no active control, four studies compared metformin with active controls (rosiglitazone, glyburide, pioglitazone, or glipizide), and one study included treatment arms that randomised to either metformin, diet and lifestyle modifications, or other antidiabetic therapies. The risk of bias in included studies varied; two studies were abstract-only publications and were judged to have a high risk of bias in most domains. Other included publications were judged to have a low risk of bias in most domains. Across comparisons, GRADE evaluations for most outcomes were judged as low or very low certainty, except for those relating to side effects, tolerance, and withdrawals, which were judged as moderate certainty. The evidence suggests that compared to placebo, metformin may result in i) a slightly smaller decline in kidney function (3 studies, 505 participants: MD 1.92 mL/min, 95% CI 0.33 to 3.51; I2 = 0%; low certainty), ii) very uncertain effects on the incidence of kidney failure (1 study, 753 participants: RR 1.20, 95% CI 0.17 to 8.49), iii) little or no effect on death (3 studies, 865 participants: RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.32; I2 = 0%; moderate certainty), iv) little or no effect on the incidence of serious adverse events (3 studies, 576 participants: RR 1.15, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.72; I2 = 0%; moderate certainty), and v) likely higher incidence of intolerance leading to study withdrawal than placebo (4 studies, 646 participants: RR 2.19, 95% CI 1.46 to 3.27; I2 = 0%; moderate certainty). The certainty of the evidence for proteinuria was very uncertain. Compared to other active controls (rosiglitazone, glyburide, pioglitazone, or glipizide), metformin i) demonstrated very uncertain effects on kidney function decline, ii) may result in little or no difference in death (3 studies, 5608 participants: RR 0.95 95% CI 0.63 to 1.43; I2 = 0%; low certainty), iii) probably results in little or no difference in intolerance leading to study withdrawal (3 studies, 5593 participants: RR 0.92, 95% CI, 0.79 to 1.08; I2 = 0%; moderate certainty), iv) probably results in little or no difference in the incidence of serious adverse events (2 studies, 5545 participants: RR 1.16, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.71; I2 = 0%; moderate certainty), and v) may increase the urinary albumin-creatinine ratio (2 studies, 3836 participants: MD 14.61, 95% CI 8.17 to 21.05; I2 = 0%; low certainty). No studies reported the incidence of kidney failure.
AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: This review highlights the lack of RCTs reporting on the effects of metformin on kidney function, particularly in patients with CKD. Future research in this field requires adequately powered RCTs comparing metformin to placebo or standard care in those with CKD. Seven ongoing studies were identified in this review, and future updates, including their findings, may further inform the results of this review.

documents.title: Update on the Efficacy and Safety of Sodium-Glucose Co-Transporter 2 Inhibitors in Patients with Chronic Diseases: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
documents.abstract: Background: Sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors have emerged as vital medications for the management of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Numerous studies have highlighted the cardioprotective and renal protective benefits of SGLT2 inhibitors. Consequently, it is essential to assess their efficacy and safety in patients with chronic diseases. Method: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating the effects of SGLT2 inhibitors on major cardiovascular and safety outcomes in patients with T2DM, heart failure (HF), and chronic kidney disease (CKD). We searched the PubMed, Cochrane, and Embase databases for trials published between 30 September 2021 and 17 May 2023. The primary outcomes of interest included nonfatal myocardial infarction (MI), hospitalization for heart failure (HHF), cardiovascular death, and nonfatal stroke. The safety outcomes assessed were hypoglycemia, urinary tract infections (UTIs), and acute kidney injury (AKI). Result: We identified 13 RCTs involving 90,413 participants. In patients with T2DM, SGLT2 inhibitors significantly reduced the risk of nonfatal MI by 12% (hazard ratio [HR] = 0.88, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.78-0.98), HHF by 33% (HR = 0.67, 95% CI: 0.62-0.74), and cardiac death by 15% (HR = 0.95, 95% CI: 0.80-1.13). However, they did not significantly reduce the risk of nonfatal stroke (HR = 0.85, 95% CI: 0.75-0.95). In patients with HF, SGLT2 inhibitors reduced the risk of HHF by 28% (HR = 0.72, 95% CI: 0.66-0.77) and cardiac death by 12% (HR = 0.88, 95% CI: 0.80-0.96). For patients with CKD, SGLT2 inhibitors reduced the risk of HHF by 35% (HR = 0.65, 95% CI: 0.55-0.76) and cardiac death by 16% (HR = 0.84, 95% CI: 0.73-0.96). Regarding safety outcomes, SGLT2 inhibitors did not significantly increase the risk of hypoglycemia in patients with T2DM, HF, or CKD, nor did they increase the risk of urinary tract infections (UTIs) in patients with HF or CKD, or the risk of acute kidney injury (AKI) in patients with HF. However, they did increase the risk of UTIs by 8% (risk ratio [RR] = 1.08, 95% CI: 1.01-1.16) in patients with T2DM and reduced the risk of AKI by 22% (RR = 0.78, 95% CI: 0.67-0.89) and 19% (RR = 0.81, 95% CI: 0.69-0.97) in patients with T2DM and CKD, respectively. Conclusions: SGLT2 inhibitors have demonstrated a significant improvement in cardiovascular outcomes for patients with T2DM, HF, and CKD while also maintaining a favorable safety profile. These findings advocate for the broader application of SGLT2 inhibitors in the management of chronic diseases, particularly in reducing the incidence of nonfatal MI, HHF, and cardiac death. Further research is essential to optimize their use across diverse patient populations and stages of disease.

Abstract Background: Sodium–glucose co-transporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors have emerged as vital medications for the management of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Numerous studies have highlighted the cardioprotective and renal protective benefits of SGLT2 inhibitors. Consequently, it is essential to assess their efficacy and safety in patients with chronic diseases. Method: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating the effects of SGLT2 inhibitors on major cardiovascular and safety outcomes in patients with T2DM, heart failure (HF), and chronic kidney disease (CKD). We searched the PubMed, Cochrane, and Embase databases for trials published between 30 September 2021 and 17 May 2023. The primary outcomes of interest included nonfatal myocardial infarction (MI), hospitalization for heart failure (HHF), cardiovascular death, and nonfatal stroke. The safety outcomes assessed were hypoglycemia, urinary tract infections (UTIs), and acute kidney injury (AKI). Result: We identified 13 RCTs involving 90,413 participants. In patients with T2DM, SGLT2 inhibitors significantly reduced the risk of nonfatal MI by 12% (hazard ratio [HR] = 0.88, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.78–0.98), HHF by 33% (HR = 0.67, 95% CI: 0.62–0.74), and cardiac death by 15% (HR = 0.95, 95% CI: 0.80–1.13). However, they did not significantly reduce the risk of nonfatal stroke (HR = 0.85, 95% CI: 0.75–0.95). In patients with HF, SGLT2 inhibitors reduced the risk of HHF by 28% (HR = 0.72, 95% CI: 0.66–0.77) and cardiac death by 12% (HR = 0.88, 95% CI: 0.80–0.96). For patients with CKD, SGLT2 inhibitors reduced the risk of HHF by 35% (HR = 0.65, 95% CI: 0.55–0.76) and cardiac death by 16% (HR = 0.84, 95% CI: 0.73–0.96). Regarding safety outcomes, SGLT2 inhibitors did not significantly increase the risk of hypoglycemia in patients with T2DM, HF, or CKD, nor did they increase the risk of urinary tract infections (UTIs) in patients with HF or CKD, or the risk of acute kidney injury (AKI) in patients with HF. However, they did increase the risk of UTIs by 8% (risk ratio [RR] = 1.08, 95% CI: 1.01–1.16) in patients with T2DM and reduced the risk of AKI by 22% (RR = 0.78, 95% CI: 0.67–0.89) and 19% (RR = 0.81, 95% CI: 0.69–0.97) in patients with T2DM and CKD, respectively. Conclusions : SGLT2 inhibitors have demonstrated a significant improvement in cardiovascular outcomes for patients with T2DM, HF, and CKD while also maintaining a favorable safety profile. These findings advocate for the broader application of SGLT2 inhibitors in the management of chronic diseases, particularly in reducing the incidence of nonfatal MI, HHF, and cardiac death. Further research is essential to optimize their use across diverse patient populations and stages of disease.
